title: What could the ECB remove from a sovereign spread?
summary: On 6 September the ECB offered to buy short-dated government bonds in circumstances where fear of a euro exit was disrupting lending across the currency union. It left its policy rates unchanged. Draghi made a distinction with consequences for anyone pricing Spanish or Italian debt. A bond yield could reflect poor national policies and the quality of the borrower’s credit as well as investors’ fear of being repaid in another currency. The ECB saw a monetary-policy case for intervening against the second risk. Investors would still have to assess the first. That gives the announcement a different meaning for two countries with equally wide sovereign spreads but different prospects of securing and complying with a support programme (opening statement and final questions on sovereign yields).

Outright Monetary Transactions, or OMTs, would take place in the secondary market. The ECB set no advance ceiling on the amount it could purchase. It also gave no numerical yield at which it would buy. In the Q&A Draghi pointed to sovereign yields, credit default swap spreads, bid–ask spreads, trading liquidity and volatility as evidence the Council would consider together. Distortion could extend in both directions, including to bonds bought by investors seeking safety. That matters when interpreting a spread against Germany. A fall in the spread can arise through a lower yield on the distressed bond, a higher yield on the benchmark, or both. The two legs should be recorded individually before drawing an inference about how much cheaper it became for a government to borrow.

The purchases would concentrate on bonds with between one and three years left to maturity. An originally ten-year bond could fall within that window. Draghi connected this segment to the short-term policy rate, the rates used in private lending and the influence of short rates farther along the curve. An investor could therefore examine where on the curve sovereign spreads changed most, including just beyond the eligible maturities. The terms did create a potential incentive for governments to issue shorter debt. Draghi acknowledged the incentive and pointed to the cost of disturbing a balanced maturity profile. Future issuance choices remained open at the meeting.

The scale of intervention depended on decisions taken outside the ECB. Governments had to pursue an appropriate EFSF or ESM programme with effective conditions. Draghi discussed both a full adjustment programme and a precautionary credit line with extensive conditions. The IMF’s help in designing conditionality was sought. Decisions about the monetary intervention remained with the Governing Council. Purchases could stop once transmission was restored or if the country failed to comply. Asked whether Spain would receive purchases before a near-term refinancing need, Draghi assigned the next move to the government and the Eurogroup. Countries already under adjustment, including Portugal and Ireland, could be considered as they regained market access. There was no common start date for purchases in those countries.

These terms also changed what a private bondholder could infer about recovery in a restructuring. Draghi said the Eurosystem would accept equal treatment with other creditors on OMT purchases. He explicitly excluded legacy Securities Markets Programme holdings from that assurance. He also committed to greater disclosure about OMT holdings. The Council had one dissenter. The source supports treating September as the announcement of a conditional buyer with the capacity to take large positions. It supplies neither a purchase amount executed that day nor an observed change in the probability of a euro exit.

The monetary and economic figures explain why transmission mattered even with inflation above target. Output contracted by 0.2% quarter on quarter in the second quarter following no growth in the first. Staff lowered both annual growth ranges, to −0.6% to −0.2% for 2012 and −0.4% to 1.4% for 2013. August inflation reached 2.6%, up from 2.4% in July, largely on higher energy prices in euros. Staff raised the inflation ranges to 2.4%–2.6% for 2012 and 1.3%–2.5% for 2013. The Council still saw moderate underlying pressures and expected inflation to fall below 2% during 2013. A further intensification of financial stress could weaken demand and domestic prices. Draghi said the previous rate cut had already anticipated cyclical weakness.

The credit data set a demanding test for OMT. Adjusted private-sector lending grew only 0.5% year on year in July. Corporate loans contracted 0.2%, while household loans grew 1.1%. M3 grew 3.8%, but the ECB associated the acceleration with increased demand for liquid balances, including faster M1 growth. Weak expenditure and balance-sheet repair reduced demand for loans. Fragmented markets and thin bank capital constrained supply in some countries. A sovereign spread might narrow immediately if investors revised the risk of currency breakup. Whether that translated into lower borrowing costs for a firm, and whether the firm actually borrowed, were separate outcomes that would need separate evidence.

questions.question: Which part of a sovereign spread moved when the terms became known?
questions.detail: Match one-, two-, three- and longer-dated yields in exposed countries to German yields at the same maturities. Examine each yield, bid–ask spreads and credit protection around the release and Q&A. This would distinguish a rally in exposed short bonds from an unwind of safe-haven demand. It would still leave fiscal credit risk and euro-exit risk partly entangled.

questions.question: How much did credible access to a support programme matter?
questions.detail: Construct a dated record of government requests, Eurogroup decisions and programme reviews, preserving what investors could know at each point. Compare issuers at similar maturities with different routes to eligibility. An improvement concentrated after credible government commitments would bear on the market value of the ECB’s conditional promise.

questions.question: Did less sovereign stress reach borrowers that relied on banks?
questions.detail: Pair national bank funding and lending rates with small-business borrowing costs and loan quantities over subsequent months. Use lending surveys to identify movements in standards and demand, and distinguish banks with different capital constraints. Easier funding followed by cheaper loans but flat volumes would have a different implication for transmission than falling sovereign yields alone.

questions.question: Did debt managers shift funding toward the eligible window?
questions.detail: Compare issuance and redemption schedules by residual maturity before and after the announcement. Separate a change in the maturity of new issues from old bonds naturally rolling into the window. A sustained change toward short funding would affect rollover exposure and could alter the interpretation of subsequent steepening in national yield curves.
